stemMd:
A long row of shallow glass cases along the gallery's north wall ______ the ledgers that survived the 1943 fire.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanationMd:
Find the true subject by stripping out every prepositional phrase. Remove "of shallow glass cases" and "along the gallery's north wall" and the sentence reduces to "A long row ______ the ledgers".

The subject is "row", which is singular, so the verb must be singular: *holds*. Choice B.

The trap is the plural noun "cases" sitting right before the blank. A noun inside a prepositional phrase is never the subject of the sentence, so it cannot control the verb. Check your answer by reading the stripped sentence aloud: "A long row holds the ledgers" sounds right, and "A long row hold the ledgers" does not.

distractorRationale.a: This is the plural present form, which agrees with "cases" instead of with the real subject "row". The words "of shallow glass cases" are a prepositional phrase and cannot supply the subject.
distractorRationale.d: This is plural as well, so it repeats the same agreement error, and the present perfect also shifts the sentence from describing the gallery as it is to describing a stretch of past time.
distractorRationale.b: The present progressive "are holding" is plural, so it makes the same agreement error, and it suggests a temporary action rather than the permanent arrangement the sentence describes.

accessibilityText: Choose the verb form that agrees with the subject in the sentence "A long row of shallow glass cases along the gallery's north wall blank the ledgers that survived the 1943 fire."
